title: Diagonal criterion for representable stack morphisms
statement: Let $S$ be a scheme [def-pc-scheme]. Stacks, Deligne--Mumford stacks, algebraic spaces and 2-fibre products have the conventions of [def-sfb-stable-pointed-moduli-groupoids, def-trf-algebraic-space]. Representable by algebraic spaces means that every scheme base change is equivalent to an algebraic space. Properties of such maps are tested on these algebraic-space base changes. Let $f:\mathcal X\to\mathcal Y$ be a morphism of Deligne--Mumford stacks over $S$ which is representable by algebraic spaces. Then $\Delta_f:\mathcal X\to\mathcal X\times_{\mathcal Y}\mathcal X$ is representable by schemes, is a monomorphism, and is locally quasi-finite [pqf-def-quasifinite] after every scheme base change. The following are equivalent: the algebraic-space maps $T\times_{\mathcal Y}\mathcal X\to T$ are separated for all schemes $T\to\mathcal Y$; $\Delta_f$ is a closed immersion after every scheme base change [def-weil-closed-immersion]; $\Delta_f$ is proper after every scheme base change [def-weil-proper-morphism]. Separated for algebraic spaces means that their relative diagonal is a closed immersion, tested after every scheme base change. A representable diagonal is a monomorphism here when each of its scheme base changes is a monomorphism, equivalently injective on all functors of points.

proof.text: A Deligne--Mumford stack is an algebraic stack for the Isom-space theorem: its representable surjective etale scheme atlas is smooth on scheme tests by the etale-implies-smooth lemma and the definitions of the two atlas properties. Thus that theorem applies to both $\mathcal X$ and $\mathcal Y$, without a finite-type hypothesis. Fix a scheme $U$ and a map $U\to\mathcal X\times_{\mathcal Y}\mathcal X$, given by $x_1,x_2\in\mathcal X(U)$ and $\alpha:f(x_1)\xrightarrow{\sim}f(x_2)$. Put $I=\operatorname{Isom}_{\mathcal X,U}(x_1,x_2)$ and $J=\operatorname{Isom}_{\mathcal Y,U}(f(x_1),f(x_2))$. These are algebraic spaces by the Isom-space theorem. On a $U$-scheme $V$, the pullback $D=U\times_{\mathcal X\times_{\mathcal Y}\mathcal X}\mathcal X$ has objects $(z,u,v)$ with $u:z\xrightarrow{\sim}x_1|_V$, $v:z\xrightarrow{\sim}x_2|_V$ and $\alpha|_V f(u)=f(v)$. Set $\beta=vu^{-1}$; then $f(\beta)=\alpha|_V$. An arrow to $(z\prime,u\prime,v\prime)$ satisfies $u\prime r=u$ and $v\prime r=v$, so is uniquely $r=(u\prime)^{-1}u$ and exists exactly when the two values of $\beta$ agree. Every $\beta$ has representative $(x_1|_V,1,\beta)$. Thus this groupoid is equivalent to the discrete sheaf of these $\beta$. Pulling back the isomorphisms pulls back this description, so the identification is natural on $U$-schemes. Thus $D=U\times_{\alpha,J}I$ as a sheaf, so it is an algebraic space by existence of space fibre products.

proof.text: The map $I\to U$ is locally of finite type by the Isom-space theorem. The composite $I\xrightarrow{q}J\to U$ is this structure map. Apply cancellation of local finite type for algebraic spaces to conclude that $q$ is locally of finite type. The algebraic-space base-change clause of the finite-type calculus then shows that $D=U\times_J I\to U$ is locally of finite type. The base-change theorem explicitly agrees with the ordinary algebraic-space notion, so it applies to $q:I\to J$ without any extra hypothesis on $f$.

proof.text: Representability of $f$ makes it faithful on every fibre groupoid. Indeed, for $z\in\mathcal X(V)$, an automorphism $\gamma$ with $f(\gamma)=1$ determines the arrow $(\gamma,1)$ of $(z,1)$ in $\mathcal X\times_{\mathcal Y,f(z)}V$: the 2-fibre-product compatibility is exactly $1= f(\gamma)$. The equivalence with the discrete algebraic space supplied by representability is fully faithful, so it identifies the automorphism group of $(z,1)$ with the singleton identity group. Hence $(\gamma,1)=(1,1)$ and $\gamma=1$. If $f(\beta)=f(\beta\prime)$, apply this observation to $(\beta\prime)^{-1}\beta$. Consequently for each $V\to U$ there is at most one $\beta$ above $\alpha|_V$. The map $D\to U$ is therefore a monomorphism of sheaves. The local-finite-type monomorphism theorem now gives separatedness and chartwise local quasi-finiteness of $D\to U$. The separated locally quasi-finite schemehood theorem applies because the target $U$ is a scheme, and represents $D$ by a scheme. Taking the identity chart of this scheme gives ordinary local quasi-finiteness of $D\to U$. Since $U$ was arbitrary, this proves all three assertions about $\Delta_f$.

Assume $\Delta_f$ is a closed immersion after all scheme base changes. For any scheme $T\to\mathcal Y$, write $A=\mathcal X\times_{\mathcal Y}T$, an algebraic space by representability. A scheme $V\to A\times_T A$ gives two pairs $(z_1,\theta_1)$ and $(z_2,\theta_2)$ with $\theta_i:f(z_i)\xrightarrow{\sim}y|_V$. Its pullback of $\Delta_{A/T}$ has sections exactly the isomorphisms $\beta:z_1\to z_2$ with $\theta_2 f(\beta)=\theta_1$. These are the sections of the pullback of $\Delta_f$ along $(z_1,z_2,\theta_2^{-1}\theta_1)$. The section identification commutes with every restriction $V\prime\to V$, so it identifies the sheaf pullbacks as maps over $V$. That scheme map is a closed immersion by assumption. Every scheme test of $\Delta_{A/T}$ is thus a closed immersion, so $A\to T$ is separated by the definition in the statement.

source.place: Tag 04YS (lemma-representable-separated-diagonal-closed), last paragraph; explicit calculation of the base-change diagonal.

proof.text: Conversely, assume $\mathcal X\times_{\mathcal Y}T\to T$ is separated for every scheme $T\to\mathcal Y$. For the arbitrary triple $(x_1,x_2,\alpha)$ over $U$ from step 1 take $y=f(x_2)$ and $A=\mathcal X\times_{\mathcal Y,y}U$. It has two sections $s_1=(x_1,\alpha)$ and $s_2=(x_2,1)$. The sheaf pullback of $\Delta_{A/U}$ by $(s_1,s_2):U\to A\times_U A$ consists exactly of isomorphisms $\beta:x_1\to x_2$ with $f(\beta)=\alpha$. This identification commutes with restriction, and by step 1 it identifies the pullback map with $D\to U$. Separatedness of $A\to U$ says precisely that this scheme test of its diagonal is a closed immersion. Therefore every scheme test of $\Delta_f$ is a closed immersion, proving the equivalence of the first two conditions.

source.place: Tag 04YS (lemma-representable-separated-diagonal-closed), scheme base-change test with the explicit two sections; same diagonal identity as equation-diagonal.

proof.text: By step 3, every scheme base change $D\to U$ of $\Delta_f$ is a monomorphism between schemes. Apply the proper-monomorphism criterion to that very scheme map: $D\to U$ is a closed immersion if and only if it is proper and a monomorphism. The monomorphism is already known, so this is equivalent to properness alone. Quantifying over all scheme maps $U\to\mathcal X\times_{\mathcal Y}\mathcal X$ proves equivalence of the second and third conditions. Together with steps 4 and 5 this proves all the stated equivalences.
